cardDescription: A human-centered, fullstack application that interfaces with an LLM to help users manage their home maintenance tasks.
caseStudyTitle: Home Maintenance Management App Case Study
tagLine: An interactive, fullstack home maintenance management prototype that uses Google Gemini to help users manage home maintenance tasks.
objective: Design and build a human-AI system that promotes explainability, trust, and a positive user experience when managing home maintenance tasks.
requirements: Display the optimal layout for the app depending on the device's screen size.
Manage access with login authentication.
View all and upcoming tasks on the user dashboard
Add tasks for tracking with an AI assistant.
Set task frequencies, reminders, and custom notes for each task.
Update or delete tasks on tasks' dedicated details pages.

learnings.title: Identifying needs through user research
learnings.insight: Research was performed through a user needs survey to better understand the current ways users manage their home maintenance tasks and identify their common pain points. Most participants responded that they rely, at least partially, on mental notes to manage up to ten tasks of various frequencies, and they shared that they often struggle to remember to perform their tasks when they had originally planned. Through quantitative and qualitative analysis, the problem space was confirmed, and requirements were defined for developing a user-centered tool that helps users set up and manage their home maintenance needs.

learnings.title: Form validation and authentication with Flask
learnings.insight:
On the login screen, users are prompted to enter a username and password to gain access to the rest of the application. On the front-end, form validation checks that users have entered a valid username and password before permitting them to move forward, and an informative error message helps users recover if they have entered incorrect credentials. Additionally, a state variable, managed with React Context, holds users on the login screen until they have entered the correct credentials, preventing users from bypassing this screen with url manipulation.

Then, on the back-end, HTTPBasicAuth's "login_required" decorator prevents users that have not entered the correct credentials from accessing the app's custom APIs that manage the flow of data within the application. With multiple layers of security, these features aim to simulate protecting user data and prevent misuse of this prototype application.

learnings.title: Chat scripting with dialog nodes
learnings.insight: When users want to set up tasks for tracking, they click or tap the blue "+" button to open up the chat modal. This feature resembles digital messaging systems, where system and user responses are presented as a scrollable dialog. Stored in a JSON file, this dialog is structured as a series of node objects, with each node having a node id, dialog text, a response type (either multiple choice or free response), multiple choice options (if applicable), and pointers to the next node based on user input. As users interact with the chat, the system follows the dialog script and sends requests to the back-end accordingly.

learnings.title: Prompt engineering and grounding with web search
learnings.insight:
Users are prompted to either describe a task that they would like to track or request task recommendations from the application. Users' inputs are subsequently inserted into one of two pre-structured prompts for sending through the Gemini API. These prompts were engineered to encourage the Gemini API to return data in a predictable format that can be programmatically handled by the back-end application.

Additionally, with the "google_search" tool enabled, responses are grounded in real web results. Metadata for where the AI system sourced its response are returned with the system's output and is also processed by the back-end. Providing these citations to users, at the time of query and on each task's details page, promotes explainability and trust in the AI system.

learnings.title: Creating custom API endpoints with Flask
learnings.insight:
Custom API endpoints were developed with Flask to handle communication between the application and the Google Gemini API and to manage CRUD operations of task data. For example, when the user types out a task for tracking in the chat, the application fetches a response from the "get_task_details" endpoint. This endpoint inserts the task name into the appropriate prompt, sends it through the Gemini API, parses the returned response, updates a JSON file with the new task, and returns the task details to the front-end.

Other endpoints help manage the flow of data within the app, like updating task frequencies, setting reminders, and adding custom notes. Users can perform these actions within the chat and from their tasks' details pages. If users decide that they no longer wish to manage a task, they can remove the task with the "Delete Task" button at the bottom of its details page. To protect users from unintentionally deleting task data, a confirmation modal promotes safety by prompting the user to confirm the action. If they do so, the "delete_task" endpoint handles removing the data from the JSON file. Overall, these endpoints provide flexibility for users to personalize their task management in the way that best fits their home maintenance needs as they change.

learnings.title: Performing usability testing
learnings.insight:
Usability testing was performed to evaluate the effectiveness of the human-AI system, identify opportunities for improvement, and assess the overall user experience. After the front-end was deployed on GitHub Pages and the back-end on Vercel, users were provided a script for setting up home maintenance tasks and encouraged to think aloud as they worked through the study. When they were finished, they were encouraged to complete a post-study survey to reflect on their experiences.

Users rated the usability of the system highly and believe it provides the right kind of utility to help them achieve their home maintenance management needs. They also identified some opportunities for increased customizability to further improve their user experiences, like being able to strike through or mark off tasks when they are completed and being able to edit AI content to better align with their specific home systems. For a future iteration of this project, these quality of life updates will be a priority for empowering users to manage their home systems with ease.

learnings.title: Future work
learnings.insight:
This prototype serves as a demonstration of how users would go about setting up home maintenance tasks for tracking with an AI assistant. It is not currently set up to handle multiple users' data, nor is it set up to send push notifications of reminders or sync with users’ calendar applications.

If this prototype were to be further developed and deployed as a real product, I would first explore creating a database with CouchDB to store JSON files of task details for individual users. Next, I would work on setting up push notifications to make task reminders functional. Then, I would add more customizability to give users more flexibility in managing their tasks. This would include functionality like dismissing reminders or marking tasks as complete, editing AI task descriptions and step-by-step instructions, and editing task reminder dates. With these changes, this AI-powered solution should help users effectively manage all of their home maintenance tasks in a way that best aligns with their individual needs and preferences.

cardDescription: A responsive, fullstack application that uses machine learning to provide users with personalized movie recommendations.
tagLine: An interactive, fullstack movie recommendation website built with Python, Flask, TypeScript, and React.js.
objective: Design and build a user-centered movie recommendation system that uses collaborative filtering to provide users with personalized movie recommendations.
requirements: Display the optimal layout for the app depending on the device's screen size.
Scroll through popular movies within the selected MovieLens dataset.
Search movies within the dataset with search bar filtering.
Browse movies within the dataset using a dropdown menu.
Rate selected movies between 0.5 and 5.
See personalized movie recommendations based on the user's rating history.

learnings.title: Data collection and environment setup
learnings.insight: After deciding to build my recommender system with collaborative filtering, I downloaded a MovieLens dataset from GroupLens with over 100,000 ratings across 9,000 movies for 610 users. I then set up a virtual environment, installed libraries like Pandas, NumPy, and Scikit-learn, and performed some data exploration to better understand the dataset.

learnings.title: Building the recommender model
learnings.insight: To implement collaborative filtering, I first used scikit-learn's cosine similarity function to identify similar users to the current user. Then, I generated recommendations by compiling a list of highly rated movies by similar users, filtering out movies that the current user has already rated, and serving up the top 10 from the filtered list. I initially used matrix factorization as the basis for my model because it is less memory intensive and accounts well for latent factors; however, I decided to pivot after assessing its performance metrics and finding it required an unreasonable number of ratings before its recommendations became relevant.

learnings.title: Creating API endpoints
learnings.insight: In order to connect the model to my front-end application, I used Flask to create custom API endpoints that handled posting new user ratings and getting new movie recommendations. Additionally, I created endpoints that communicated with the OMDb API to get movie poster images and plot summaries for recommended movies. My most rewarding takeaway from this phase of the project was learning how to efficiently test these endpoints with Insomnia - an awesome open-source application for testing and troubleshooting APIs.

learnings.title: Deploying the fullstack application
learnings.insight: I hosted my front-end application on GitHub Pages, but I needed a different solution for hosting the backend since GitHub Pages does not support hosting server-side code. I chose to use PythonAnywhere's free tier to deploy my backend application and used its server/error logs to troubleshoot issues that had not occured during local testing. PythonAnywhere was really easy to learn and use, and I look forward to using it again for future fullstack projects.

cardDescription: A highly interactive personal finance application using TypeScript, React.js, Tailwind CSS and Chart.js.
tagLine: A responsive, interactive personal finance application using TypeScript, React.js, Tailwind CSS and Chart.js.
objective: Per the design brief from Frontend Mentor, build a webpage that allows users to:
requirements: See all of the personal finance app data at-a-glance on the overview page.
View all transactions on the transactions page with pagination for every ten transactions.
Search, sort, and filter transactions.
Create, read, update, delete (CRUD) budgets and saving pots.
View the latest three transactions for each budget category created.
View progress towards each pot.
Add money to and withdraw money from pots.
View recurring bills and the status of each for the current month.
Search and sort recurring bills.
Receive validation messages if required form fields aren't completed.
Navigate the whole app and perform all actions using only the keyboard.
Display the optimal layout for the interface depending on the device's screen size.
See hover and focus states for all interactive elements on the page.

learnings.title: Make data accessible throughout application with context
learnings.insight: Since the JSON data of account balances, transactions, budgets and pots are accessed on multiple levels throughout the application, I used context to provide pages and components with a single source of truth. With the createContext hook, I imported the JSON data, created constant variables of balances and transactions, and initialized state variables of budgets and pots. By providing these variables and relevant state updating functions to the full app, all pages are ensured to reflect the latest additions, updates, or deletions of state data.

learnings.title: Define reusable and configurable UI components
learnings.insight: With repeated styling calls across multiple components, like the white background with fixed padding and rounded corners for almost every component, one of my main focuses for this project was on building reusable wrappers and UI components. I defined props to handle variants of dropdowns, buttons and section headings, and I am continuing to refine my component tree and improve code readability.

learnings.title: Create cohesive search, sort, and filter elements
learnings.insight: For the Transactions and Recurring Bills pages, I used context again to ensure any combination of search, sort, and filtering inputs would be reflected in the search results. I created a utility file and defined functions to help with these operations, from relatively straightforward search and filter functions to multiple bubble sorting algorithms to handle the different sorting options.

learnings.title: Build budgets doughnut chart using Chart.js
learnings.insight: I wanted to gain experience using a good data visualization library, so I used Chart.js to build my budgets doughnut chart. Although this was only one component in my application, I really liked how configurable and easy-to-use the chart was. I am definitely looking forward to finding more use cases for Chart.js in future projects.

learnings.title: Handle page navigation with HashRouter, Links, useEffect and useLocation
learnings.insight: As with all projects I deploy to GitHub Pages, I set up my project with HashRouter and Links to navigate between the pages of my application. However, I initially ran into an issue where refreshing on any page would disconnect the page per the URL and page stored in context. I had been updating the page in context whenever a Link was clicked, but, after realizing that refreshing the page resets the context, I decided to pivot to changing the page in context whenever the URL changes. By using the pathname of useLocation as a dependency for my useEffect hook, I was able to ensure that the app always knows its current page.

cardDescription: A responsive, pixel-perfect website for a fictional e-commerce company using TypeScript and React.js.
tagLine: An interactive, scalable e-commerce website with pixel-perfect styling.
objective: Provided with a Figma design file, build a Audiophile e-commerce website that empowers users to:
requirements: Display the optimal layout for the app depending on the device's screen size.
Add/Remove products from the cart.
Edit product quantities in the cart.
Fill in all fields in the checkout.
See correct checkout totals depending on the products in the cart.
See an order confirmation modal after checking out with an order summary.

learnings.title: Define SPA routing with React Router DOM
learnings.insight: Created routing between the homepage, category pages, product pages, and checkout page with HashRouter (since BrowserRouter is not compatible with GitHub Pages). Used Link to connect navigation links and CTAs to their respective pages, and used the useParams hook to build a back button to move up from product pages to their respective category page. With dynamic path parameters, this e-commerce site could easily be scaled up with more products by simply adding more objects to the JSON data file.

learnings.title: Use context to manage shared state
learnings.insight: Created two context providers to manage shared state across the site: CartContext and UserProgressContext. The CartContext manages adding items to the cart from the product pages, removing items from inside the cart modal, and updating quantities of products from both locations. The UserProgressContext then handles the user's movement throughout the main site and modals such as the mobile navigation menu, cart, and checkout confirmation. It also performs a validation check on the checkout form, preventing the user from progressing to the checkout confirmation before completing all of the required fields.

learnings.title: Develop useful client-side form validation
learnings.insight: Setting users up for success with informative error messages is critical in preventing frustration and improving the overall user experience. For this form, I set up regex patterns to make sure user inputs matched valid formats for email addresses, phone numbers, and payment details, and I defined a general validation check to make sure no field is left empty. I set error messages to only be displayed to the user after they click away from the input field, giving them a chance to fill out the form correctly before being guided towards a valid input as needed. The submit button them becomes clickable only after all fields are validated, which is important for maintaining user trust particularly when handling their payment information.

learnings.title: Incorporate Tailwind CSS styling
learnings.insight: Practiced using the popular CSS framework, Tailwind CSS, to bolster maintainability and speed of implementing future updates. Gained experience using responsive utility variants, and looking forward to learning more about directives and reusing styles.
